catalog_quote: Sanie also shows typical Eastern Yi vowel and tone systems. For example, it has a high rising tone corresponding to the high level tone of most other nearby Eastern Yi languages, including Nasu, Samei and Samataw. This distinguishes these languages and the Northern Yi languages from the rest of the languages spoken by the Yi nationality, which have a low creaky tone in the same words. The degree of dialect differentiation within Sanie is very great, despite the small distances involved.

new_statements.quote: [...] tones as reconstructed in Bradley (1979, 1991). Of course there are also some conditioned splits and sandhi changes which affect the reflexes of these tones; for example some prefixed *2 tone syllables have Sanie [33] tone rather than [21] tone. One can see that all three languages share the high level or rising pitch reflex of *L tone (Matisoff 1972), as in Nasu of northern Yunnan and northwesternmost Weining in Guizhou and in Nosu of Sichuan. This is also found in some environments in [...] Sani, Lisu, Lahu and other Ngwi Group languages; for example the well-known [35] reflex of some *L tone [...]. Table 2. Ngwi Group prototones - Sanie / Samataw / Samei: *H 53 / 35 / 53; *L 45 / 55 / 55; *1 44 / 21 / 44; *2 21/33 / 33 / 21; *3 33 / 44 / 33. [elsewhere:] '... tonal splits conditioned by prefix and initial combinations.'

new_statements.relation_note: Tone only: five tone values for Sanie in a proto-tone correspondence table (53, 45, 44, 21/33, 33) with remarks on splits and sandhi; no stress/accent statement visible in any snippet window and none indexed.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Sanie is a lexical-tone Ngwi language: Bradley gives five Sanie tone values as reflexes of the Proto-Ngwi categories (*H > 53, *L > 45 high rising, *1 > 44, *2 > 21 (33 after some prefixes), *3 > 33), notes conditioned tonal splits by prefix/initial and sandhi affecting *2 syllables, and groups Sanie with Samataw, Samei, Nasu and Nosu by the high level/rising reflex of *L; nothing is said about word stress or accent (a probe for 'stress'/'stressed' with 'Sanie' in the volume returns no match).
new_statements.exceptions: sandhi: some prefixed *2-tone syllables have [33] rather than [21]; conditioned tonal splits by prefix and initial combinations; strong dialect differentiation within Sanie (Zhaozong conservative, Qitai in south-central Tuanjie 'particularly extreme')
new_statements.identity_note: OUR-BIBLIOGRAPHY WORK ('likely states stress; not yet obtained', De Gruyter paywall), added: a TONE statement and tone-correspondence table read through Google Books full-text snippets of the issue volume 'Language Endangerment in the Sinosphere' (id PRNiAAAAMAAJ, no preview). The article is Bradley's first-hand account of Sanie (Bai Yi/Sa'nguie west of Kunming: Zhaozong, Tuanjie/Qitai etc. named in the snippets), and besides the sociolinguistics it carries a compact phonological characterisation: initial series vs Nasu, rhyme reflexes, [ɿ] allophone of /i/, 'tonal splits conditioned by prefix and initial combinations', and Table 2 with Sanie, Samataw and Samei reflexes of the five Proto-Ngwi tone categories. The Sanie column (53, 45, 44, 21/33, 33) is consistent with Bradley 2006 p.117 already held by the project (Sanie high rising 45 = Nasu/Samei/Samataw high level 55 < *L). Snippet reconstruction: column alignment follows the header order Sanie | Samataw | Samei as printed in two independent snippets; gaps marked. No open copy found (Unpaywall closed per A; RG blocked; web search on the exact title found none).
